blocks.html: Logistic regression models the log-odds of a binary outcome as a linear function of predictors. Odds and the odds ratio are recalled first (§13.2.1), then the logit (§13.2.2), the binary model (§13.2.3), its assumptions (§13.2.4), adjustment and interaction (§13.2.5), and how to read the output (§13.2.6). The section ends with the variants for ordered (§13.2.7), unordered (§13.2.8) and individually matched (§13.2.9) outcomes.
Odds and Odds Ratio

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The odds of an event are p ÷ (1 − p) (recall §5.5.3). The odds ratio (OR) is the odds of the event in one group divided by the odds in another (recall §10.6.4). It says how many times higher or lower the odds are in the first group.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Odds and probability move in the same direction but are different numbers. An OR is a ratio of odds, not of probabilities. It approximates the risk ratio only when the outcome is rare in both groups (recall §10.6.4). Logistic regression works on odds because of the logit (§13.2.2).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: If 20% of CBHI members in one group drop out, their odds of dropout are 0.2 ÷ 0.8 = 0.25 (“1 to 4”). If 10% drop out in a comparison group, their odds are 0.1 ÷ 0.9 = 0.111. OR = 0.25 ÷ 0.111 = 2.25: the odds of dropout are 2.25 times as high in the first group. The risk ratio is 0.2 ÷ 0.1 = 2.0. With a 10–20% outcome the two already differ.

points.html: OR = 1: no difference in odds. OR > 1: higher odds in the first (usually exposed) group. OR < 1: lower odds.
Do not read an OR as “times as likely”. That is risk-ratio language, and it is wrong unless the outcome is rare.
exp(coefficient) from a logistic regression is an OR for a one-unit increase in that predictor, holding the other predictors constant (§13.2.3).

blocks.html: The Logit Transformation

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The logit of a probability p is its log-odds: logit(p) = ln[p ÷ (1 − p)]. It maps probabilities between 0 and 1 onto the whole real line.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: This is the transformation §13.1 asked for. As p approaches 0 the logit heads to −∞; as p approaches 1 it heads to +∞. A straight line on the logit scale can therefore never give an impossible probability.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: p = 0.5 has odds 1 and logit ln(1) = 0, the midpoint. p = 0.9 has odds 9 and logit ln 9 = 2.197. p = 0.1 has odds 1/9 and logit −2.197. The scale is symmetric about zero.

blocks.alt: The logistic (sigmoid) curve linking the logit to a probability
blocks.caption: Figure 13.1. The logistic (sigmoid) curve linking the logit to a probability.

points.html: Model: logit(p) = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + … The logit is the link function (recall §13.1) of logistic regression.
Back-transform with the inverse logit: p = 1 ÷ (1 + e^(−logit)). Plotted against a predictor, p traces the S-shaped curve of Figure 13.1; the logit itself is a straight line.
The model assumes linearity on the logit scale, not the probability scale. §13.2.4 shows how to check it.

blocks.html: Binary Logistic Regression

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Binary logistic regression models the log-odds of one category of a two-category outcome (coded 1, the “event”) as a linear function of the predictors, fitted by maximum likelihood (recall §13.1).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
The simplest form of logistic regression: yes/no, member/non-member, died/survived. The likelihood extends the coin of §13.1. Household i has its own probability pᵢ, given by the inverse logit of its linear predictor. A member contributes pᵢ to the likelihood and a non-member contributes 1 − pᵢ:

L = Π pᵢ^(yᵢ) (1 − pᵢ)^(1 − yᵢ),

where Π (capital pi) means “multiply together over all households”, as Σ means “add up”, and a power of yᵢ = 1 or 0 keeps or drops that factor.

Software searches for the b’s that make L largest. There is no closed-form answer as there is for least squares, so the search is iterative.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In the CBHI survey (500 households in 20 villages, 25 per village; 150 members, 30%), regress membership on distance to the nearest facility alone. The fitted coefficient for distance is −0.162 per km, so OR = e^(−0.162) = 0.85: each extra kilometre multiplies the odds of membership by 0.85.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cb <- read.csv("data/cbhi_survey.csv")
m0 <- glm(cbhi_member ~ distance_km, family = binomial, data = cb)
summary(m0)$coefficients
exp(cbind(OR = coef(m0), confint.default(m0)))
              Estimate Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)  0.3367709 0.24028160  1.401568 1.610444e-01
distance_km -0.1622277 0.03098085 -5.236387 1.637501e-07
                   OR     2.5 %    97.5 %
(Intercept) 1.4004182 0.8744393 2.2427755
distance_km 0.8502476 0.8001556 0.9034754

The Estimate column is on the log-odds scale: −0.162 per km. The Wald z is the estimate ÷ its SE (−0.162/0.031 = −5.24). exp() turns the coefficient and its Wald CI (b ± 1.96 SE) into the OR: 0.85 (95% CI 0.80 to 0.90). This is the crude OR; §13.3 adjusts it. The intercept, 0.34, is the log-odds of membership at 0 km.

points.html: The outcome has exactly two categories, coded 0 and 1. The choice of which is 1 sets the direction of every OR, so state it.
Estimation is by maximum likelihood, not least squares.
Several predictors enter exactly as in multiple regression (§13.2.5).

blocks.html: Assumptions of Logistic Regression

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Logistic regression assumes: a linear relation between each continuous predictor and the log-odds; independent observations; no severe multicollinearity; and enough events for the number of coefficients, with no predictor that separates the outcome perfectly.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Some conditions carry over from linear regression in modified form (recall §12.3): linearity, independence, multicollinearity. Others are specific to a binary outcome: the number of events and separation. Normality of residuals and constant variance do not apply. A 0/1 outcome has binomial variance p(1 − p), which the model already builds in.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A model of CBHI membership on distance assumes that the log-odds of membership fall in a straight line with distance. To check it, add a quadratic term (distance²) and see whether the fit improves; or group distance into categories and see whether the log-odds of each category lie roughly on a line. §13.3 does the first.

points.html: Linearity in the logit: for each continuous predictor, on the log-odds scale, not the probability scale (which is S-shaped by design).

Independence: broken when observations come in clusters (households in a village) or as repeated measures on one person (recall §5.4). Clustered binary data need the methods of §15.2 (models that allow for correlation within clusters).
Multicollinearity: checked with the VIF, as in linear regression (recall §12.4.4).

Events per variable (EPV): a common convention asks for at least 10 events per estimated coefficient. It comes from a simulation in which no major problems occurred at EPV ≥ 10 (Peduzzi et al., 1996). Later simulations found acceptable bias and coverage below 10 in many settings (Vittinghoff & McCulloch, 2007), and prediction-model work recommends calculating the required size rather than using a rule of thumb (Riley et al., 2019). Treat EPV < 10 as a warning about overfitting (a model that fits the chance quirks of this sample and so predicts poorly in new data), not a bar.
Separation: if a predictor (or combination) perfectly predicts the outcome, the MLE does not exist. The coefficient runs off towards ±∞ and software prints a huge OR with a huge SE (§13.2.6).

blocks.label: Checkpoint 13.1

questions.prompt: A colleague fits a logistic regression and finds one predictor has an OR of 45,000 with an enormous standard error. What is the most likely explanation? Is it an error to fix with a different technique?
questions.answer: Almost certainly separation: the predictor (or a combination of predictors) perfectly or almost perfectly predicts the outcome, so the ordinary maximum likelihood estimate does not exist and the coefficient drifts towards infinity. The data are not wrong, and the 45,000 must not be reported. First look at why the predictor separates the outcome so cleanly (a coding error, a predictor that is really a consequence of the outcome, very small numbers). If the pattern is genuine, valid finite estimates can be obtained with Firth’s penalised likelihood (Heinze & Schemper, 2002) or exact logistic regression.

questions.prompt: Explain what “linearity in the logit” means, and why checking it on a plot of raw probability against the predictor would be the wrong approach.
questions.answer: The model assumes that each continuous predictor has a straight-line relation with the log-odds of the outcome: logit(p) = b₀ + b₁x. On the probability scale the correctly specified model is S-shaped, so a curved probability plot is expected and says nothing about whether the assumption holds. Check on the logit scale instead: add a quadratic term (or a spline) and see whether the fit improves, or group the predictor and see whether the log-odds of the groups lie roughly on a line.

questions.prompt: Of 20 children screened, 5 are anaemic. Write the likelihood for the prevalence p, find the MLE, and give its logit. What probability corresponds to a logit of 1.2?

blocks.note: (Answers in the Appendix at the end of the book.)

blocks.html: Multivariable Logistic Regression

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Multivariable logistic regression includes two or more predictors at once. Each exponentiated coefficient is an adjusted OR: the OR for that predictor, holding the others in the model constant.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
This is the step from simple to multiple regression (recall §12.4), taken on the logit scale. Adding a confounder to the model adjusts the exposure’s OR for it (recall §12.4.1).

Two features are new.

Noncollapsibility. A linear regression coefficient does not change when you add a predictor that is unrelated to the exposure. An OR can. Even with no confounding, the adjusted (conditional) OR can differ from the crude (marginal) one. So a crude-versus-adjusted comparison of ORs mixes confounding with noncollapsibility (Pang et al., 2013). The worked calculation below shows the direction: with a non-confounding covariate, adjustment moves the OR away from 1. A shift towards 1 after adjustment therefore points to confounding, though it does not prove it.

Interaction on two scales. Interaction (effect modification) means the effect of one factor differs by the level of another (recall §12.4.3, §11.7). Logistic and Poisson models test interaction on the multiplicative scale: is the joint ratio equal to the product of the separate ratios? Public health often needs the additive scale: do the excess risks add? Additive interaction shows where an intervention prevents the most cases. For public-health purposes the additive scale “is thus useful in targeting specific populations and in resource allocation” (Knol & VanderWeele, 2012). The two scales can give different answers on the same data.

The relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI) measures additive interaction from relative risks, with the group exposed to neither factor as the reference:

RERI = RR₁₁ − RR₁₀ − RR₀₁ + 1.

RERI = 0 means the excess risks add exactly; RERI > 0 means the joint effect is more than additive.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
RERI. Let R₀₀, R₁₀, R₀₁, R₁₁ be the risks with neither factor, only A, only B, and both. If the excess risks add, then R₁₁ − R₀₀ = (R₁₀ − R₀₀) + (R₀₁ − R₀₀). Divide by R₀₀: RR₁₁ − 1 = (RR₁₀ − 1) + (RR₀₁ − 1). The departure from additivity is RR₁₁ − 1 − (RR₁₀ − 1) − (RR₀₁ − 1) = RR₁₁ − RR₁₀ − RR₀₁ + 1 = RERI. Only relative risks are needed, which is why RERI can be computed from a regression model.

Noncollapsibility. Take two equal-sized strata of a covariate, exposure equally common in each (so the covariate is not a confounder), and an OR of exactly 2 in both. Unexposed risk: 0.1 in stratum 1, 0.5 in stratum 2. Exposed odds are twice the unexposed odds: 2 × 0.111 = 0.222 (risk 0.182) and 2 × 1 = 2 (risk 0.667). Pooled, the risks are 0.300 (unexposed) and 0.424 (exposed). Crude OR = (0.424/0.576) ÷ (0.300/0.700) = 1.72. The adjusted OR is 2.00, further from 1 than the crude 1.72, with no confounding at all.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In a hypothetical 5-year cohort of 4,000 adults, 1,000 in each group, the risk of type 2 diabetes (per 1,000) is 20 with neither obesity nor a family history, 40 with obesity only, 60 with a family history only, and 120 with both (Figure 13.2).

blocks.caption: Figure 13.2. Five-year diabetes risk per 1,000 in four groups (hypothetical). If the excess risks added, the “both” group would have 20 + 20 + 40 = 80 per 1,000; if the risk ratios multiplied, 20 × 2 × 3 = 120. The observed 120 shows no multiplicative interaction but a clear additive one.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Risk ratios against “neither”: RR₁₀ = 40/20 = 2, RR₀₁ = 60/20 = 3, RR₁₁ = 120/20 = 6.
  2. Multiplicative scale: RR₁₁ ÷ (RR₁₀ × RR₀₁) = 6 ÷ 6 = 1. No interaction.
  3. Additive scale: RERI = 6 − 2 − 3 + 1 = 2. Strong positive interaction.
  4. In cases: obesity alone adds 20 cases per 1,000, family history alone adds 40. Together they add 100, which is 40 more than 20 + 40. If these associations are causal, weight-reduction effort among people with a family history prevents the most diabetes per person reached.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
d <- data.frame(obese = c(0, 1, 0, 1), famhx = c(0, 0, 1, 1),
                cases = c(20, 40, 60, 120), n = 1000)
m <- glm(cbind(cases, n - cases) ~ obese * famhx,
         family = binomial, data = d)
round(exp(cbind(OR = coef(m), confint.default(m))), 2)
b <- coef(m)
OR10 <- exp(b[2]); OR01 <- exp(b[3]); OR11 <- exp(b[2] + b[3] + b[4])
c(RERI_OR = unname(OR11 - OR10 - OR01 + 1))
              OR 2.5 % 97.5 %
(Intercept) 0.02  0.01   0.03
obese       2.04  1.18   3.52
famhx       3.13  1.87   5.23
obese:famhx 1.05  0.56   1.97
 RERI_OR 
2.512492

obese * famhx fits both main effects and their product. The product term’s OR (1.05, CI 0.56 to 1.97) is the multiplicative-scale interaction; it is close to 1, so a reader who looked only at this line would say “no interaction”. RERI computed from the model’s ORs is 2.51, larger than the risk-based 2.0 because the outcome reaches 12% in the “both” group. Knol & VanderWeele (2012) warn that “when the outcome is common… using ORs may exaggerate interaction measures”; the risk-ratio models of §13.7 avoid this.

points.html: An adjusted OR must be reported with what it was adjusted for.

Noncollapsibility: crude and adjusted ORs can differ without confounding. When the covariate is not a confounder, adjustment tends to move the OR away from 1. A move towards 1 is more suggestive of confounding, but still not proof. Choose confounders on subject-matter grounds (recall §11.6), not by the change they produce.

Report interaction on both scales, with the stratum-specific estimates and a single reference category (Knol & VanderWeele, 2012). A product term in a logistic model tests multiplicative interaction only.
RERI = RR₁₁ − RR₁₀ − RR₀₁ + 1; 0 = additivity. Computed from ORs it approximates the risk-based value only when the outcome is rare.

blocks.html: Reading Logistic Regression Output

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Reading a logistic regression table means answering five questions: what each OR means given the coding, how precise it is, what probability the model predicts for a given person, how well the model performs overall, and what the table does not show.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Coding first. Every number depends on which outcome category was coded 1 and which level of each categorical predictor is the reference.

Continuous predictors. The OR is the multiplicative change in odds per one-unit increase, and it compounds. An OR of 1.05 per year means 10 years multiply the odds by 1.05¹⁰ = 1.63, not 1.5.

CI and p-value are built on the log-odds scale, as in §12.2.4, then exponentiated. A 95% CI for an OR that excludes 1 goes with p < 0.05; 1 is the no-association value.

Predicted probability. For a given person, add up b₀ + b₁x₁ + … to get the logit, then apply the inverse logit (recall §13.2.2). This is the number a clinician can use.

Model performance. Discrimination asks whether the model gives higher predicted probabilities to people who had the event than to those who did not. Calibration asks whether the predicted probabilities are numerically right: among people predicted at 30%, do about 30% have the event? A model can have one without the other. §15.5.1 builds the ROC curve and its area (AUC), and §15.5.2 applies them to a model’s predicted probabilities (the c-statistic) together with calibration checks.

Failure modes. Separation (recall §13.2.4) shows up as a huge OR with a huge SE. Do not report that OR. The data are real; the ordinary MLE is the problem. Firth’s penalised likelihood gives finite estimates (Heinze & Schemper, 2002); exact logistic regression is another option. Overfitting threatens when the number of coefficients is large relative to the number of events (the EPV convention, recall §13.2.4).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
A hypothetical study of 400 patients models in-hospital death (1 = died) on age (years), sex (reference: male) and diabetes (reference: no diabetes). The table is invented for teaching, and so is the intercept, b₀ = −5.00: an illustrative value, not an estimate from real data. An OR table like this one does not show the intercept; you need it from the full model output.

Predictor OR 95% CI p-value
Age (per year) 1.04 1.02 to 1.06 <0.001
Sex: Female 0.78 0.52 to 1.17 0.23
Diabetes: Yes 2.15 1.34 to 3.45 0.002

Each additional year multiplies the odds of death by 1.04, adjusted for sex and diabetes; a 20-year gap multiplies them by 1.04²⁰ = 2.19. Women have lower odds than men, but the CI crosses 1 (p = 0.23), so the data are compatible with no difference. Diabetes is associated with about twice the odds of death (OR 2.15), adjusted for age and sex.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Predicted probability of death for a 70-year-old woman with diabetes:

  1. Convert ORs to coefficients: ln 1.04 = 0.0392 per year; ln 0.78 = −0.248; ln 2.15 = 0.765.
  2. Logit (with the illustrative b₀ = −5.00) = −5.00 + 70 × 0.0392 + (−0.248) + 0.765 = −5.00 + 2.745 − 0.248 + 0.765 = −1.738.
  3. p = 1 ÷ (1 + e^(1.738)) = 1 ÷ (1 + 5.69) = 0.15.

The model predicts a 15% chance of in-hospital death for her. A 70-year-old man without diabetes has logit −5.00 + 2.745 = −2.255 and p = 0.095. Neither number can be read off the OR column alone.

points.html: State the event coding and every reference category. An OR without them cannot be interpreted.
A per-unit OR compounds: OR^k for k units.
Discrimination and calibration are different properties; §15.5.2 measures both.

An OR is not a risk ratio. When the outcome is common (more than about 10%), the OR overstates the risk ratio if it is above 1 and understates it if below 1 (Zhang & Yu, 1998). §13.7 gives the conversion formula and models that estimate the ratio directly.
Reporting checklist: adjusted OR with 95% CI; outcome coding; reference categories and units; what was adjusted for.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 13.2

questions.prompt: A logistic regression reports an OR of 1.08 per year of age. A colleague says this means a 30-year age gap corresponds to 30 × 1.08 = 32.4-fold higher odds. What is wrong, and what is the correct figure?
questions.answer: A per-unit OR multiplies once for each unit; it does not add. The coefficient is additive on the log-odds scale (30 × ln 1.08 = 30 × 0.0770 = 2.309), so the OR for 30 years is e^2.309 = 1.08³⁰ = 10.06, about a 10-fold increase in odds, not 32.4.

questions.prompt: Two logistic models on the same data report the same OR for a predictor, but one discriminates well between cases and non-cases and the other does not. How is this possible?
questions.answer: Discrimination depends on how well all the predictors together separate people who had the event from those who did not, through the spread of the predicted probabilities. A single OR describes one predictor’s association. One model may contain other strong predictors that spread the predicted probabilities widely (good discrimination), while the other contains only weak predictors, so everyone gets a similar predicted probability (poor discrimination), even though the shared predictor’s OR is the same.

questions.prompt: In a cohort, the 1-year risk of TB is 1% in adults with neither diabetes nor undernutrition, 1.5% with undernutrition only, 2% with diabetes only and 4% with both. Compute the multiplicative interaction ratio and the RERI, and say what each means.
questions.answer: RR₁₀ (undernutrition only) = 1.5/1 = 1.5; RR₀₁ (diabetes only) = 2/1 = 2; RR₁₁ = 4/1 = 4. Multiplicative: RR₁₁ ÷ (RR₁₀ × RR₀₁) = 4 ÷ 3 = 1.33. The joint risk ratio is a third larger than the product of the separate ones: positive interaction on the multiplicative scale. Additive: RERI = 4 − 1.5 − 2 + 1 = 1.5. The excess risks would add to 0.5 + 1 = 1.5 percentage points; the observed joint excess is 3 points. Positive additive interaction: if these associations are causal, correcting undernutrition prevents more TB per person reached among diabetics (4% → 2%, 2 cases per 100) than among non-diabetics (1.5% → 1%, 0.5 per 100).

blocks.note: (Answers in the Appendix at the end of the book.)

blocks.html: Ordinal Logistic Regression

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Ordinal logistic regression (the proportional-odds or cumulative-link model) handles an outcome with three or more ordered categories. It models the odds of being in a higher rather than a lower category, across every cut-point between categories.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Ordinal outcomes (recall §1.1.2), such as disease severity or a Likert score, have an order but not equal spacing. With categories mild/moderate/severe there are two cut-points: mild vs moderate-or-severe, and mild-or-moderate vs severe. The model fits one logistic equation per cut-point with a separate intercept for each, but a single common coefficient for each predictor.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Modelling disease severity (mild/moderate/severe) on age and treatment delay: an OR of 1.5 for each week of delay means that each week multiplies the odds of being in a more severe category, at either cut-point, by 1.5.

points.html: Collapsing to a binary outcome, or ignoring the order with a multinomial model (§13.2.8), throws information away.

The proportional-odds assumption: each predictor has the same OR at every cut-point. Check it (for example by fitting separate binary models at each cut-point and comparing the ORs); if it fails, a multinomial or partial-proportional-odds model is an alternative.
Statistical software fits it as an “ordered logistic” (proportional-odds) model. Declare the outcome as ordered first (recall §1.6).

blocks.html: Multinomial Logistic Regression

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Multinomial logistic regression handles an outcome with three or more unordered categories. It models the odds of each category relative to a chosen reference category.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Blood group or cause of death has no natural order. With k categories, the model fits k − 1 logistic equations at once, each comparing one category with the reference.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Cause of under-five death (diarrhoeal disease, pneumonia, malnutrition-related, other; reference “other”) modelled on household water source and nutritional status gives three sets of coefficients: diarrhoea vs other, pneumonia vs other, malnutrition vs other. Each exponentiated coefficient is an OR (strictly a relative-risk ratio between two categories) against “other”.

points.html: Choose a substantively meaningful reference, often the largest category, and state it. Changing the reference changes every reported coefficient but not the model’s fit.
Do not use an ordinal model for unordered categories: it imposes an order that does not exist.
Binary, ordinal and multinomial logistic regression assume independent observations. Individually matched data need conditional logistic regression (§13.2.9).

blocks.html: Conditional Logistic Regression for Matched Data

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Conditional logistic regression fits a logistic model to data in matched sets (a case and its matched controls). It compares members within each set, conditioning away each set’s own baseline odds, and estimates the exposure OR from within-set contrasts only.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
In an individually matched case-control study, each case has one control (or m controls) chosen to be similar on, say, age, sex and village. Matching makes controls resemble their cases on the matching factors and, through them, on exposure. The matched sets must therefore be kept in the analysis (Pearce, 2016).

Why not ordinary logistic regression with one dummy variable per matched set? With pairs, there are almost as many dummy variables as people. This is the sparse-data problem. For 1:1 pairs, unconditional logistic regression with pair dummies gives an OR equal to the square of the correct conditional OR (Pearce, 2016). Conditional logistic regression removes the set effects from the likelihood instead of estimating them.

Only discordant pairs carry information: pairs where exactly one member was exposed. With one binary exposure, the conditional MLE is the matched-pair OR of §10.8 (recall: OR = b/c, the ratio of the two kinds of discordant pair). The regression form adds what §10.8 cannot do: adjustment for further covariates that were not matched on, and 1:m matching.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Take one matched pair, one case and one control, where exactly one member is exposed. Within the pair, the exposed member has odds ψe^β and the unexposed member odds ψ, where ψ is the pair’s own baseline odds and e^β is the OR. Given that exactly one of the two is a case, the probability that the case is the exposed member is

e^β ÷ (1 + e^β),

and ψ has cancelled. Concordant pairs (both or neither exposed) give a probability that does not involve β, so they drop out. With b pairs in which the case is exposed and c pairs in which the control is exposed, the conditional likelihood is

L(β) = [e^β/(1 + e^β)]^b × [1/(1 + e^β)]^c.

This is the coin of §13.1 with “heads” = the case is the exposed member: the MLE of e^β/(1 + e^β) is b/(b + c), which gives e^β̂ = b/c. SE(ln OR) = √(1/b + 1/c).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A district case-control study of infant diarrhoea matched each of 80 cases to one control of the same age and village. Exposure: not exclusively breastfed (not-EBF). Of the 80 pairs, 16 had both exposed, 30 neither, 24 had only the case exposed (b) and 10 only the control exposed (c).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Matched OR = b/c = 24/10 = 2.40.
  2. SE(ln OR) = √(1/24 + 1/10) = 0.376.
  3. 95% CI = exp(ln 2.40 ± 1.96 × 0.376) = 1.15 to 5.02.
  4. Ignoring the matching: pooled, 40 of 80 cases and 26 of 80 controls were exposed, so OR = (40 × 54)/(40 × 26) = 2.08. Breaking the pairs gives a smaller OR, closer to 1, here.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(survival)
mc <- read.csv("data/matched_casecontrol.csv")
cl <- clogit(case ~ not_ebf + strata(pair_id), data = mc)
summary(cl)
Call:
coxph(formula = Surv(rep(1, 160L), case) ~ not_ebf + strata(pair_id), 
    data = mc, method = "exact")

  n= 160, number of events= 80 

          coef exp(coef) se(coef)     z Pr(>|z|)  
not_ebf 0.8755    2.4000   0.3764 2.326     0.02 *
...
        exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
not_ebf       2.4     0.4167     1.148     5.019
...
Likelihood ratio test= 5.94  on 1 df,   p=0.01
Wald test            = 5.41  on 1 df,   p=0.02
Score (logrank) test = 5.76  on 1 df,   p=0.02

strata(pair_id) tells clogit which rows form a matched set. coef is ln OR = 0.8755 = ln(24/10), with SE 0.376 = √(1/24 + 1/10), step 2. exp(coef) is the OR of 2.40 with CI 1.15 to 5.02, step 3. The score test statistic (5.76) is McNemar’s χ² for these pairs (recall §10.8: (b − c)²/(b + c) = 196/34 = 5.76). clogit is built on the Cox model of Chapter 14, which is why the call says coxph; you do not need survival analysis to use it. Further covariates are added after not_ebf in the formula.

points.html: Individually matched sets (pairs, 1:m, siblings, neighbours): conditional logistic regression. Frequency (group) matching on broad categories such as 5-year age groups: ordinary logistic regression that includes the matching variables (Pearce, 2016; Kuo et al., 2018).
Matching does not remove confounding by the matching factors in a case-control study. It must still be accounted for in the analysis (Pearce, 2016).
Only discordant sets contribute. 80 pairs with 34 discordant is effectively a study of 34 pairs.
The matching variables themselves cannot be studied as risk factors: their effect is conditioned away.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 13.3

questions.prompt: A multinomial model of cause of under-five death uses “other” as the reference. How would the reported results change if “pneumonia” were the reference, and what would stay the same?
questions.answer: Every set of coefficients would now compare a category with pneumonia (diarrhoea vs pneumonia, malnutrition vs pneumonia, other vs pneumonia) instead of with “other”, so all the reported ORs change in value and meaning. The model’s fit, its predicted probabilities for each category, and its likelihood are unchanged: the reference is a reporting choice, and any comparison can be recovered from either parameterisation (e.g. diarrhoea vs pneumonia = (diarrhoea vs other) ÷ (pneumonia vs other)). State the reference.

questions.prompt: Why is ordinal logistic regression a mistake for an unordered outcome such as blood group?
questions.answer: The ordinal model estimates cumulative odds across cut-points in a fixed order (for example A < B < AB < O) and forces one OR per predictor across all cut-points. Blood groups have no order, so the cut-points, the cumulative odds and the single OR are all artefacts of an arbitrary ordering. A different arbitrary order would give different results. A multinomial model is the right one.

questions.prompt: In a 1:1 matched case-control study of 100 pairs, 30 pairs have only the case exposed and 12 have only the control exposed. Compute the matched OR and its 95% CI. What would an unconditional logistic model with 99 pair dummies report?
questions.answer: OR = b/c = 30/12 = 2.5. SE(ln OR) = √(1/30 + 1/12) = √0.1167 = 0.342. 95% CI = exp(ln 2.5 ± 1.96 × 0.342) = exp(0.916 ± 0.670) = 1.28 to 4.88. Unconditional logistic regression with a dummy for each pair suffers from sparse data; for 1:1 pairs it gives the square of the conditional OR (Pearce, 2016): 2.5² = 6.25, a serious overestimate.
